subject: Medicine
topic: Nosocomial Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI) Prevention
stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted to the general medical floor with mild community-acquired pneumonia. She is awake, alert, and oriented x 4. She has mild urinary incontinence for which she wears disposable incontinence pads at home. During admission intake, the bedside floor nurse places a transurethral indwelling Foley catheter, documenting on the chart: "Placed Foley catheter to manage urinary incontinence and prevent skin breakdown." On hospital day 4, the patient develops a fever of 38.6°C (101.5°F), suprapubic tenderness, and cloudy urine draining into the collection bag. Urine culture grows > 100,000 CFU/mL of multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae. In reviewing this adverse healthcare-associated infection, which of the following represents the most effective institutional strategy to prevent future catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs)?

options.text: Administer daily prophylactic oral nitrofurantoin throughout the duration of urinary catheterization
options.explanation: Routine antimicrobial prophylaxis during catheterization does not prevent CAUTI, increases adverse drug toxicity, and rapidly breeds multidrug-resistant organisms.

options.text: Perform routine bladder irrigation with sterile chlorhexidine or neomycin solutions every 12 hours
options.explanation: Bladder irrigation disrupts the closed sterile drainage system, irritates mucosal tissue, and increases bacteremia and infection rates.

options.text: Replace the entire Foley catheter and drainage bag routinely every 72 hours over a guidewire
options.explanation: Routine scheduled catheter changes cause urethral trauma, introduce external pathogens, and fail to reduce CAUTI rates.

options.text: Place all incontinent female hospital admissions in permanent indwelling catheters upon floor arrival
options.explanation: Universal catheterization for incontinence is directly contrary to national safety standards and exponentially drives hospital-acquired CAUTI outbreaks.

options.text: Establish strict clinical criteria for catheter insertion, avoid catheters for incontinence management, and implement daily nurse-driven removal protocols
options.explanation: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) are the most frequent healthcare-associated infections worldwide. Pathogens ascend the intraluminal catheter drainage tube or along the extraluminal mucous sheath between the catheter and urethral mucosa. The risk of developing bacteriuria increases cumulatively by 3% to 7% for EVERY SINGLE DAY an indwelling catheter remains in place; by day 30, virtually 100% of catheterized patients are colonized. Guidelines from the CDC and the Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America (SHEA) outline clear evidence-based prevention principles: (1) RESTRICT INSERTION TO VALID INDICATIONS: Valid indications include acute urinary retention, hourly fluid monitoring in critically ill ICU patients, perioperative use for specific surgeries, assistance with healing deep sacral pressure wounds, and end-of-life comfort care. FOLEY CATHETERS SHOULD NEVER BE PLACED FOR THE CONVENIENCE OF STAFF OR FOR ROUTINE INCONTINENCE MANAGEMENT. (2) PROMPT REMOVAL: The single most effective intervention to prevent CAUTI is to REMOVE THE CATHETER AS SOON AS IT IS NO LONGER MEDICALLY NECESSARY. Implementing daily multidisciplinary catheter review checklists and nurse-driven discontinuation protocols significantly lowers CAUTI incidence and hospital costs.

explanation: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) are the most frequent healthcare-associated infections worldwide. Pathogens ascend the intraluminal catheter drainage tube or along the extraluminal mucous sheath between the catheter and urethral mucosa. The risk of developing bacteriuria increases cumulatively by 3% to 7% for EVERY SINGLE DAY an indwelling catheter remains in place; by day 30, virtually 100% of catheterized patients are colonized. Guidelines from the CDC and the Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America (SHEA) outline clear evidence-based prevention principles: (1) RESTRICT INSERTION TO VALID INDICATIONS: Valid indications include acute urinary retention, hourly fluid monitoring in critically ill ICU patients, perioperative use for specific surgeries, assistance with healing deep sacral pressure wounds, and end-of-life comfort care. FOLEY CATHETERS SHOULD NEVER BE PLACED FOR THE CONVENIENCE OF STAFF OR FOR ROUTINE INCONTINENCE MANAGEMENT. (2) PROMPT REMOVAL: The single most effective intervention to prevent CAUTI is to REMOVE THE CATHETER AS SOON AS IT IS NO LONGER MEDICALLY NECESSARY. Implementing daily multidisciplinary catheter review checklists and nurse-driven discontinuation protocols significantly lowers CAUTI incidence and hospital costs. Prevent Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTI - CDC Guidelines): - EPIDEMIOLOGY: Most common hospital-acquired infection. Daily risk of bacteriuria is 3-7% PER DAY of catheterization. - APPROPRIATE INDICATIONS FOR FOLEY CATHETER: 1. Acute urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction; 2. Accurate hourly urine output measurement in critically ill ICU patients; 3. Perioperative use for specific urologic/pelvic surgeries; 4. Healing of open stage 3-4 sacral/perineal pressure ulcers in incontinent patients; 5. Comfort care in terminal palliative patients. - INAPPROPRIATE INDICATIONS: Convenience of staff, routine incontinence management, or uncooperative patients. - SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE PREVENTION STRATEGY: AVOID PLACEMENT IF POSSIBLE, AND REMOVE CATHETER IMMEDIATELY WHEN NO LONGER MEDICALLY INDICATED (daily nurse-driven protocol).
